creative.body:
I had given myself 3 enemas in 6 days before I finally admitted to myself something was deeply wrong.

The Miralax had stopped working at week 7. The magnesium had stopped working at week 9. By week 11 I was on suppositories. By week 13 I was on enemas. I'm 56 years old. On Wegovy. Down 33 pounds. And I had become a woman who could not make her own body work without a tube and a bottle in her bathroom at midnight.

This is the story of how I climbed that ladder, and the night I stopped climbing.

Week 7.

The first time the Miralax stopped working.

I had been on it since week 5. 1 capful in the morning, 1 in the evening, in a glass of water with breakfast and dinner. It had been doing the job. Not perfectly, not gently, but the job. Then on a Tuesday morning of week 7 I drank it and nothing happened. Wednesday, nothing. Thursday, nothing.

I called my GI's nurse line. The nurse came back on the line after talking to the doctor and told me to double the dose. I asked if that was safe. She said, "Just stay on it. It's perfectly safe. You can be on Miralax indefinitely."

I went to CVS that afternoon and bought a second bottle. I started taking 2 capfuls in the morning and 2 in the evening.

It worked. For about a week and a half.

Week 9.

Magnesium citrate.

A woman in a Wegovy Facebook group told me that magnesium was the natural alternative to Miralax. She said it was gentle. She said her sister had been on it for 2 years.

I bought a bottle. The label said do not exceed 350mg per day.

I started at 400mg.

Within 4 nights I was at 600. Within 2 weeks I was at 1,200mg every night, on top of the doubled Miralax in the morning. The bottle had a warning printed on it in 2 colors. I covered the warning with my thumb whenever I picked the bottle up off my counter, the way you cover a number on a scale you do not want to read.

It worked. Until it didn't. The dose I started on stopped doing what it used to do, which is exactly what the bottle of Miralax had done 2 weeks earlier, in a different bottle, in a different aisle.

Week 11.

Dulcolax suppositories.

I called the GI again. The nurse said the doctor was calling something into my CVS. She did not say what. I drove there at 9pm in sweatpants and a hoodie because I did not want to run into anyone I knew.

The pharmacist handed me a small white box and did not make eye contact. I did not make eye contact either. I paid with a card and walked out.

I sat in my car in the CVS parking lot for 5 minutes before I drove home, looking at the box on the passenger seat.

I used 1 that night. It worked.

I used another 4 days later. It half-worked.

I used a third 3 days after that. Nothing.

The bottle of suppositories went into the cabinet under the sink, behind the cleaning supplies, where my husband would not see them.

Week 13.

Saline enemas at the 24-hour Walgreens.

It was 11pm on a Wednesday. The CVS by my house was closed. I drove the 14 minutes to the 24-hour Walgreens on the highway because the next-closest 24-hour pharmacy was 30 minutes away and I could not wait 30 minutes.

Sweatpants. Hoodie. Hood up.

I walked in. I went to the wrong aisle on purpose first, the one with the cold medicine, and stood there pretending to read a box of Mucinex for 4 minutes. Then I walked over to the laxative aisle and stood there with my back to the cameras and read the boxes.

I picked up a 4-pack.

I walked to the front. The cashier was a woman maybe 25 years old. She scanned the box and put it in a plastic bag without looking at me. I paid with a card and walked out without saying anything.

I sat in my car in the Walgreens parking lot and cried with my forehead on the steering wheel for 6 minutes before I could put the car in drive.

I drove home. I went into the bathroom and locked the door even though my husband was already asleep. I sat on the floor in front of the toilet on a folded towel with my phone propped against the bathtub and watched a YouTube video on how to give yourself a saline enema.

I cried the entire time the video was playing.

I cried the entire time I gave myself the enema.

It worked. Barely.

I gave myself a second one 4 days later.

I gave myself a third 2 days after that.

Then the 4th enema sat on the counter.

I had pulled it out of the box. I had put it on the bathroom counter next to the sink. I had locked the bathroom door. It was 2am.

I did not use it.

I did not call anyone. I did not call my husband upstairs. I did not call my doctor in the morning. I did not call my sister.

I sat on the bathroom floor with my back against the tub and stared at the bottle on the counter for an hour. The grout between the tiles I was sitting on had a coffee stain I had never noticed before. I kept looking at the bottle and looking at the stain and looking at the bottle.

Somewhere in that hour I said, out loud, to nobody, "If you use this, you are not going to stop. You are going to be the woman who uses these every 2 days for the rest of her life. And you are going to keep calling people who do not have an answer. And you are going to spend the next 8 years climbing a ladder you have already been climbing for 6 weeks."

I stood up at 3am and put the unused 4th enema in a plastic grocery bag and tied the top.

I did not take the bag out to the garbage. I carried it down to the garage and set it on a shelf above the recycling bin.

Then I came back upstairs, sat down at my kitchen table with my phone, and began the 8 nights that changed everything.

I read for 8 nights straight. Not in any order. Not by topic. I went where the threads sent me. Reddit posts that linked to old gastroenterology forums that linked to PubMed abstracts that linked back to patient comment sections on motility blogs. I read women writing in real time about their own escalation ladders, identical to mine, in the same order, on the same medications, by the same doctors. I read a motility specialist's reply on a thread at 4am that said, in 11 words, "Your doctor has been treating the wrong organ for 13 weeks." I read about laxative dependency, the actual medical term, used in case studies, applied to women whose natural motility was gone, who were on weekly hospital cleanouts, who had been climbing my ladder for 8 years longer than I had. I read about apigenin and pulled up the studies on smooth-muscle contractility. I read about the difference between celery powder and standardized celery extract. I read about why a capsule is the wrong delivery format for a stomach that has stalled. I read about chlorophyllin and sulfur compounds and what was actually happening every afternoon at 4pm under my ribs. By the 8th night I had a single page of handwritten notes next to my coffee cup and the entire mechanism had clicked into place.

The medication works in 2 places. Not 1.

The appetite suppression happens in my brain. That is the engine of the weight loss. That is why I had lost 33 pounds. That is the part I did not want to undo.

But the medication takes the stomach from normal to nearly frozen. Food that should leave in 4 hours sits there for 10 or 12. While it sits there, bacteria ferment it. The bloating, the pressure, the constipation, the brick that will not pass, every single symptom I had been suffering through was coming from my stomach. Not my colon.

Stomach at the top. 6 feet of intestine in between. Colon at the bottom.

The food was stuck at the top.

Miralax works on the colon. Magnesium works on the colon. Dulcolax works on the colon. Saline enemas work on the colon. Every product I had escalated through, in every aisle of every drugstore, works on the same organ.

6 feet downstream from where the actual problem was sitting.

There was nothing in my colon to flush. The food was still trapped 6 feet upstream. Every product I had used was forcing a movement out of whatever scraps reached my colon. That was why each one had stopped working sooner than the last. That was the entire dependency curve.

I had been treating the wrong organ for 13 weeks.

What works on the right organ is apigenin. Plant compound concentrated in celery, working on the smooth muscle of the stomach wall, gently helping the contractions start again. Not a laxative. Not a stimulant. Does not produce dependency. Does not override the medication. The brain part, the engine of the weight loss, is not touched. Apigenin only works on the stomach side effect.

With chlorophyllin, which binds the sulfur compounds the bacteria are producing in the stalled stomach, neutralizing the bloating at the source.

With a small targeted dose of soluble prebiotic fiber for the lower gut once the upstream was moving. Not bulk-forming. Not Metamucil. Grams, not handfuls.

I ordered Motilli on the morning after the 8th night. Standardized apigenin extract from celery, not powder. Chlorophyllin and the soluble prebiotic. 2 heart-shaped gummies a day. 90-day money-back guarantee. Small batch.

The first 4 days on the bottle, nothing. The second week the pressure under my ribs eased. By the third week I went on my own for the first time since week 7. By week 6 the Miralax, the magnesium, the suppositories, the unopened enemas, all of it was off my bathroom counter. My husband saw the empty counter and said, "Took you long enough."

I have not given myself another enema. I have not used another suppository.

The unused 4th enema is still in the grocery bag in my garage.

I have not taken it to the curb.

I walk past it every morning on the way to my car.

Sometimes I look at it and feel relief. Sometimes I look at it and feel rage. Sometimes I look at it and feel something I do not have a word for, which is the closest thing to pride I have ever felt about my own body.

I keep walking past it because as long as it is sitting on that shelf, I remember exactly what 2am on the bathroom floor felt like, and I remember exactly what the woman who stopped climbing did instead.

creative.title: Miralax Failed. Magnesium Failed. Suppositories Failed. Then Came The Enemas.
